read.sections.0.text.note: Back-translation check: 'aplikasi pesanan' for 'messaging apps': 'pesanan' can also mean an order. Check whether 'aplikasi mesej' or 'aplikasi pesanan ringkas' is clearer.
read.sections.0.text.back: Messages spread very fast through phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some are honest mistakes and some are completely made up. A message in capital letters that says “Share now” can feel urgent, but that does not make it true. To judge a claim, first identify the source of that claim. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so nobody can know where it came from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, and it is dated today. It also gives evidence: the exact times and a clear reason for the closure. A clear source with specific details is usually more trustworthy.
read.sections.0.text.source: Messages spread very fast on phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some are honest mistakes and some are completely invented. A message with capital letters that says “Share now” can feel urgent, but that does not make it true. To judge any claim, first identify its source. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so nobody can tell where it really came from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, and it is dated today. It also gives evidence: exact times and a clear reason for the closure. A clear source with specific details is usually more trustworthy.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Messages move fast on phones. Some are true. Some are not true. A post in capital letters that says “Share now” can feel important. But that does not make it true. When you see a claim, ask about its source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the centre itself. It has a date. It also has evidence, such as the exact times. So Post B is easier to trust.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Messages move fast on phones. Some are true. Some are wrong. A post in big letters that says “Share now” can feel important. But that does not make it true. When you see a claim, ask about the source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the centre itself. It has a date. It also has evidence, like exact times. So Post B is easier to trust.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Check the date and the context

read.sections.1.text.back: Even a real picture can mislead people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the picture is from last year, so it cannot tell us anything about tomorrow. The date, place and reason a picture was taken are its context, and context changes the meaning of the picture. Pictures can also be edited with apps, or even made by a computer. The edges of the giant fish in Message F look strange, and nobody else has a picture of it. When a picture or story looks shocking, look for the same news from other trusted sources.
read.sections.1.text.source: Even a real photo can mislead people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the photo is from last year, so it cannot tell us anything about tomorrow. The date, the place and the reason for a photo are its context, and context changes what a photo means. Photos can also be edited with apps, or even made by a computer. The giant fish in Message F looks strange at the edges, and nobody else has a picture of it. When a photo or story seems surprising, look for the same news from another trusted source.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: A real picture can still trick you. Post C shows a real door. But the picture is from last year. It does not show tomorrow. The time and place a picture was taken are its context. Context can change the meaning of a picture. Some pictures are changed with apps. Some are made by a computer. The big fish in Message F looks strange. Nobody else has a picture of it. Look for the news somewhere else that you trust.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: A real photo can still trick you. Post C shows a real door. But the photo is from last year. It does not show tomorrow. When and where a photo was taken is its context. Context can change what a photo means. Some photos are changed with apps. Some are made by computers. The big fish in Message F looks strange. No one else has a photo of it. Look for the news in another place you trust.

read.sections.2.text.back: A rumour is a story that spreads from one person to another without evidence. Message D and Message E are both like rumours. Message D does not explain who is giving the free boots. Message E says “doctors don't want you to know”, but it does not name any doctor or health organisation. Before sharing any message, try to verify it. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was it made? What is the evidence? Then compare it with a trusted source, such as a teacher, a health worker or an official notice. If you cannot verify a message, it is usually safer not to forward it.
read.sections.2.text.source: A rumour is a story that spreads from person to person without proof. Message D and Message E are both like rumours. Before sharing any message, try to verify it. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was it made? What is the evidence? Then compare it with a trusted source, such as a teacher, a health worker or an official notice. If you cannot verify a message, it is usually safer not to forward it.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: A rumour is a story that spreads without evidence. Messages D and E are like rumours. Both messages do not say who made them. If you cannot check it, do not send it to other people.

watch.summary.note: Translator: The hedging words “think”, “likely” and “probably” became “difikirkan”, “berkemungkinan” and “mungkin”. The video stays in English, so check these are the Malay words that best show a report is not sure. Back-translation check: Translator flag stands: check that 'difikirkan', 'berkemungkinan' and 'mungkin' are the most natural Malay hedging words for 'think', 'likely' and 'probably'. 'Difikirkan' may sound awkward ('dipercayai' or 'dijangka' are other options).
watch.summary.back: This animated video is about how to choose your news. Not long ago, most people got news from a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may even disagree about facts. The video gives some tips. If possible, look for the first source, such as the actual report or speech. When a big news story is still happening, don't check every few minutes. Wait for clear facts. Read the same news in more than one place. Look for words like “thought to be”, “likely” or “maybe”. These words show that the report is not certain. Be careful when a report does not say who gave the facts. Most importantly, check a news story before you share.
watch.summary.source: This animated video is about how to choose your news. Not long ago, most people got news from a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may even disagree about the facts. The video gives some tips. When you can, find the first source, like the real report or speech. When a big story is still happening, do not check every few minutes. Wait for clear facts. Read the same story in more than one place. Look for words like “think”, “likely” or “probably”. They show that a report is not sure. Be careful when a report does not say who gave the facts. Most important, check a story before you share it.

sensitiveNotes.0.back: These examples were deliberately chosen to be ordinary and neutral: a centre closure, free shoes, a health myth and an edited picture. Do not use real rumours about sensitive topics, such as legal processes, aid or official services, in class. If a student brings up a rumour like that, do not debate its details; refer the student to the official organisation that runs that service.
